question: Define 'giving false evidence' under Section 227 of the BNS. Explain with the help of the Illustrations.
modelAnswer: Under s.227 (formerly s.191 IPC), a person gives false evidence when, being legally bound by an oath or by an express provision of law to state the truth, or being bound by law to make a declaration on any subject, he makes a statement which is false and which he knows or believes to be false or does not believe to be true. The ingredients are: (1) a legal obligation to state the truth — by oath, by an express provision of law, or by a legal duty to make a declaration; (2) a statement, whether verbal or otherwise (Expl. 1); (3) falsity of the statement; and (4) knowledge or belief of its falsity, or absence of belief in its truth. Explanation 2 makes a false statement about one's own belief false evidence: a person may be guilty by stating that he believes what he does not believe, or that he knows what he does not know. The Illustrations show the working of these rules: (a) falsely swearing that one heard Z admit B's claim is false evidence even though the claim is just; (b) stating that one believes a signature is Z's when one does not believe it is false evidence; (c) an honest statement of belief, even if mistaken, is not false evidence; (d) claiming to know Z was at a place when one knows nothing about it is false evidence, whether or not Z was there; and (e) an interpreter who gives a translation he does not believe to be true gives false evidence. The section is only a definition; punishment is under ss.229-231.

question: Distinguish between 'giving false evidence' (Section 227) and 'fabricating false evidence' (Section 228).
modelAnswer: (1) Nature: giving false evidence is making a false statement; fabricating false evidence is creating false material — a false circumstance, a false entry in a book, record or electronic record, or a document or electronic record containing a false statement. (2) Obligation: s.227 requires that the maker be legally bound by oath, law or a duty to make a declaration to state the truth; s.228 has no such requirement — anyone can fabricate. (3) Intention: s.227 needs only knowledge or belief of falsity; s.228 needs an intention that the fabricated matter appear in evidence in a judicial proceeding, a legal proceeding before a public servant, or before an arbitrator, and that it cause the decision-maker to form an erroneous opinion on a point material to the result. (4) Stage: false evidence is given when the statement is made; fabrication is complete when the false material is created with the required intention, even if never used. (5) Examples: a witness lying on oath (s.227); planting jewels in Z's box to have him convicted of theft, a false entry in a shop-book for use in court, or a forged letter placed where police will search (s.228 Illustrations). Both are punished under s.229 (seven years in a judicial proceeding, three years otherwise), and more severely under ss.230-231 when aimed at convicting someone of a grave offence.

question: What is the punishment for false evidence under Sections 229, 230 and 231 of the BNS? Explain what 'judicial proceeding' includes.
modelAnswer: Section 229(1) punishes intentionally giving false evidence in any stage of a judicial proceeding, or fabricating false evidence for use in any stage of one, with imprisonment of either description up to seven years and fine up to ₹10,000. Section 229(2) punishes intentionally giving or fabricating false evidence in any other case with up to three years and fine up to ₹5,000. Section 230(1) punishes giving or fabricating false evidence intending, or knowing it likely, to cause a person to be convicted of a capital offence, with imprisonment for life or rigorous imprisonment up to ten years, and fine up to ₹50,000; under s.230(2), if an innocent person is convicted and executed as a result, the offender may be punished with death or the s.230(1) punishment. Section 231 punishes false evidence aimed at the conviction of an offence that is not capital but punishable with life or seven years or more, with the same punishment as a person convicted of that offence. 'Judicial proceeding' is widened by the Explanations to s.229: a trial before a court-martial is a judicial proceeding (Expl. 1); an investigation directed by law preliminary to a proceeding before a court is a stage of a judicial proceeding (Expl. 2), as in an enquiry before a Magistrate on whether to commit a case for trial; and an investigation directed by a court and conducted under its authority is also a stage of a judicial proceeding (Expl. 3), as in an enquiry by an officer deputed by a court to determine land boundaries. The s.229 offences are non-cognizable and bailable; ss.230-231 are non-cognizable, non-bailable and triable by a Court of Session.

question: Explain the offence of causing disappearance of evidence under Section 238 of the BNS.
modelAnswer: Section 238 (formerly s.201 IPC) punishes whoever, knowing or having reason to believe that an offence has been committed, causes any evidence of its commission to disappear, or gives information about it that he knows or believes to be false, with the intention of screening the offender from legal punishment. The ingredients are: (1) an offence has actually been committed; (2) the accused knows or has reason to believe it; (3) he causes evidence of it to disappear, or gives false information about it; and (4) he does so with the intention of screening the offender. The punishment depends on the gravity of the original offence: (a) if punishable with death, up to seven years and fine; (b) if punishable with life or up to ten years, up to three years and fine; (c) if punishable with less than ten years, imprisonment of the kind provided for the offence up to one-fourth of its longest term, or fine, or both. The Illustration gives the example of A helping B hide the body of Z, whom B murdered, to screen him — A is liable to seven years and fine. The principal offender may also be convicted under s.238 for destroying evidence of his own crime. Mere suspicion is not enough: the prosecution must prove that an offence was committed and that the accused knew or had reason to believe it. Classification: under clause (a) cognizability follows the original offence and it is triable by a Court of Session; clauses (b) and (c) are non-cognizable; all are bailable.

question: Discuss Section 248 of the BNS (false charge of offence made with intent to injure). What changes has the BNS made?
modelAnswer: Section 248 (formerly s.211 IPC) punishes whoever, with intent to cause injury to any person, institutes or causes to be instituted any criminal proceeding against him, or falsely charges him with having committed an offence, knowing there is no just or lawful ground for the proceeding or charge. The ingredients are: (1) instituting (or causing to be instituted) a criminal proceeding, or making a false charge; (2) knowledge that there is no just or lawful ground for it; and (3) intent to cause injury to the person. 'Falsely charging' is complete once a false accusation is made to an authority competent to act on it, such as the police or a Magistrate; 'instituting a criminal proceeding' requires a proceeding to be set in motion before a court. Under clause (a), the punishment is imprisonment of either description up to five years, or fine up to ₹2 lakh, or both; under clause (b), where the criminal proceeding is instituted on a false charge of an offence punishable with death, life imprisonment or ten years or more, it is up to ten years and fine. Both clauses are non-cognizable and bailable; (a) is triable by a Magistrate of the first class and (b) by a Court of Session. The BNS significantly increases the punishment: under s.211 IPC the basic offence carried up to two years, and the aggravated offence up to seven years for false charges of offences punishable with seven years or more. The higher penalty is meant to deter the filing of false criminal cases.

question: Explain the offences of harbouring offenders under Sections 249, 253 and 254 of the BNS. What is the effect of the spouse exception?
modelAnswer: Section 249 (formerly s.212 IPC) punishes whoever, after an offence has been committed, harbours or conceals a person whom he knows or has reason to believe to be the offender, intending to screen him from legal punishment. The punishment is graded: up to five years and fine if the offence is punishable with death; up to three years and fine if punishable with life or up to ten years; and up to one-fourth of the longest term, or fine, or both, if punishable with one year but not ten years. It is cognizable and bailable. Section 253 (formerly s.216 IPC) applies where a person convicted of or charged with an offence escapes from lawful custody, or a public servant has lawfully ordered his arrest; whoever, knowing of the escape or order, harbours or conceals him to prevent his arrest is punishable with up to seven years and fine (death offence), up to three years with or without fine (life or ten years), or one-fourth of the term (lesser offences). Section 254 (formerly s.216A IPC) punishes harbouring persons known or believed to be about to commit, or to have recently committed, robbery or dacoity, intending to facilitate the crime or screen them, with rigorous imprisonment up to seven years and fine; it does not matter whether the robbery or dacoity is in India or abroad. 'Harbour' has the wide meaning in s.2 — including supplying shelter, food, money, clothes, arms or transport. All three sections contain an Exception: they do not apply where the harbouring or concealment is by the offender's spouse. The law recognises that a husband or wife cannot reasonably be expected to hand over his or her spouse, so the spouse is not punished for sheltering the offender. The exception covers only the spouse, not other relatives such as parents or siblings.

question: Explain Sections 250 and 251 of the BNS and the Exception attached to them.
modelAnswer: Section 250 (formerly s.213 IPC) punishes whoever accepts, attempts to obtain, or agrees to accept any gratification, or any restitution of property, for himself or another, in consideration of concealing an offence, screening a person from legal punishment, or not proceeding against a person to bring him to legal punishment. Section 251 (formerly s.214 IPC) punishes the other side: whoever gives, causes, offers or agrees to give or cause any gratification, or restores or causes restoration of property, to a person in consideration of that person doing any of those things. Both are graded by the gravity of the concealed offence: up to seven years and fine if punishable with death; up to three years and fine if punishable with life or up to ten years; and up to one-fourth of the longest term, or fine, or both, for lesser offences. Section 250 is cognizable; s.251 is non-cognizable; both are bailable and triable by a Magistrate of the first class. The Exception after s.251 provides that neither section applies where the offence may lawfully be compounded. Since the law itself allows parties to settle compoundable offences (listed in BNSS s.359), it would make no sense to punish the payment or receipt of compensation as part of such a settlement. But paying a witness or victim to keep quiet about a non-compoundable offence such as robbery or rape is punishable.

question: Discuss the liability of public servants who allow persons in custody to escape under Sections 259, 260, 261 and 264.
modelAnswer: The BNS distinguishes between intentional and negligent conduct, and between undertrials and convicts. Section 259 (formerly s.221 IPC) applies to a public servant legally bound to apprehend or keep in confinement a person charged with or liable to be apprehended for an offence, who intentionally omits to apprehend him, intentionally suffers him to escape, or intentionally aids his escape or attempted escape. Punishment depends on the offence charged: up to seven years (offence punishable with death), three years (life or up to ten years), or two years (less than ten years), in each case with or without fine. Section 260 (formerly s.222 IPC) applies where the person is under sentence of a court or lawfully committed to custody: life or up to fourteen years if under sentence of death; up to seven years if sentenced to life or ten years or more; and up to three years, or fine, or both, if sentenced to less than ten years or lawfully committed. Section 261 (formerly s.223 IPC) covers negligence: a public servant legally bound to keep in confinement a person charged with or convicted of an offence, or lawfully committed, who negligently suffers him to escape, is punishable with simple imprisonment up to two years, or fine, or both. Section 264 (formerly s.225A IPC) is residuary, covering cases not provided for by ss.259-261 or any other law — intentional omission or sufferance, up to three years; negligent, simple imprisonment up to two years. Most of these are cognizable; s.260(a)-(b) are non-bailable, and s.260(a) is triable by a Court of Session.

question: What is the offence under Section 269 of the BNS? How does it interact with the original case?
modelAnswer: Section 269 (formerly s.229A IPC) punishes whoever, having been charged with an offence and released on bail bond or bond, fails without sufficient cause to appear in court in accordance with the terms of the bail or bond. The burden of proving sufficient cause lies on the accused. The ingredients are: (1) the accused was charged with an offence; (2) he was released on bail bond or bond; (3) he failed to appear in court as required; and (4) he had no sufficient cause, which he must prove. The punishment is imprisonment of either description up to one year, or fine, or both. It is cognizable, non-bailable, not compoundable and triable by any Magistrate. The Explanation makes clear that the punishment is (a) in addition to the punishment to which he would be liable on conviction for the original offence, and (b) without prejudice to the court's power to order forfeiture of the bond. So a person who jumps bail can face three separate consequences: punishment for the original offence if convicted, a separate conviction under s.269, and forfeiture of the bail bond under the BNSS. Genuine reasons such as serious illness or accident may amount to sufficient cause.

question: Problem: A's son B kills a man in a road-rage incident. A washes B's blood-stained shirt, throws B's knife into a well, and hides B in A's village house. B's wife C also brings him food there. When the police ask, A tells them B was at home all night. Discuss the liability of A and C.
modelAnswer: B has committed murder (s.103), an offence punishable with death. A's liability: (1) By washing the shirt and throwing away the knife, A caused evidence of the offence to disappear, and by telling the police B was at home all night he gave information he knew to be false, both with the intention of screening B from legal punishment. This falls within s.238(a): up to seven years and fine. (2) By hiding B in his village house after the offence, knowing him to be the offender, with the intention of screening him, A harboured an offender under s.249(a): up to five years and fine. The spouse exception does not help A, since it covers only a spouse, not a parent. (3) A's false statement to the police may also be charged under s.240 (false information respecting an offence, up to two years), though s.238 is the more appropriate charge because of his intention to screen B. C's liability: by bringing food to B while he is hiding, C 'harbours' him within the s.2 definition (supplying food). But the Exception to s.249 provides that the section does not extend to harbour or concealment by the spouse of the offender, so C commits no offence under s.249. If, on the facts, C also helped destroy evidence, s.238 has no spouse exception and she could be liable under it.

question: Problem: In a pending money suit, D threatens the plaintiff's key witness E that he will harm E's daughter unless E tells the court that the loan was repaid. Out of fear, E so testifies. Discuss the liability of D and E.
modelAnswer: D's liability: D threatened E with injury to the person of someone in whom E is interested (his daughter), intending to cause E to give false evidence. This is the offence under s.232(1): imprisonment of either description up to seven years, or fine, or both. It is cognizable and non-bailable, and triable by the court that can try the offence of giving false evidence. Section 232(2) does not apply, as it applies only when an innocent person is convicted and sentenced to death or more than seven years as a result. D may also be liable for abetting E's false evidence (by instigation), and if D then relies on that evidence in the suit knowing it to be false, for corruptly using false evidence under s.233. E's liability: E, bound by oath to state the truth, made a statement in a judicial proceeding which he knew to be false. He has given false evidence under s.227, punishable under s.229(1) with up to seven years and fine up to ₹10,000. Whether E can rely on duress depends on the general exceptions: s.32 (act to which a person is compelled by threats) protects only a person compelled by threats that, at the time, reasonably cause apprehension of instant death to that person, and excludes murder and offences against the State punishable with death. A threat of future harm to his daughter does not meet that test, so E has no complete defence. The threat is, however, a strong mitigating factor at sentencing.
